On 3/22/14 11:24 AM, Marianne Espeland wrote:

Hi Nick,

I have successfully finished the majority of my
analyses in
BioGeoBears thanks to the hints you gave me a while
ago, but
ran a problem when trying a last run with a fixed
state on
the root. The favored model (DECj+stratified) gives a
geologically implausible combination of areas and I
want to
see if a model with only one ancestral area is a
much worse
fit.

I have eight areas (A-H), want to fix the root to B
and do
the following:
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$__fixnode=97
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$__fixlikes=c(0,1,0,0,0,0,0,0)

But in the results the root is not fixed to B, but
is BF as
usual, although the log-likelihood is slightly
lower. Am I
setting fixlikes wrong? Couldn't find much
documentation on
how to set it except for setting the state you want
to fix
to 1 and the others to 0.


So, 2 things:

1. Make sure the node you want is actually 97. In R's
numbering, if your tree has 96 species, the tips will be
nodes #1-96, and the root will be node 97.

2. Probably you got #1 right, but I can see an issue
with fixlikes. These specify the likelihoods of states,
i.e. geographic ranges, which are different than areas.

If you have 8 areas, you can have up to 2^8
states/ranges. You can check the numbers of states with
numstates_from_numareas, as in the example script.

You can get the list of states/ranges with these commands:


https://groups.google.com/__forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/__states_list/biogeobears/zkHP___YpA9kY/8c3vR-gIqP0J

<https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/states_list/biogeobears/zkHP_YpA9kY/8c3vR-gIqP0J>

(ignore the bit about plotting the legend, just get the
states list)

For you, assuming your areas are A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H, your
state numbers would be:

CppNum = numbering starting from 0 for C++
RNum = numbering starting from 1 for R
Range = areas in the range

==============================
CppNum RNum Range
0 1 empty, "_"
1 2 A
2 3 B
3 4 C
4 5 D
5 6 E
6 7 F
7 8 G
8 9 H
9 10 AB
10 11 AC
...
......assuming maxareas=8...
...
255 256 ABCDEFGH
==============================

Handy code:

# Get the number of ranges/states
numstates_from_numareas(8,8,__TRUE)

# Fix node 97 to range of "B"
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$__fixnode=97
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$__fixlikes = rep(0, times=256)
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$__fixlikes[3] = 1

Cheers! PS can I put this on the BioGeoBEARS google
group? Or I can X out your name/contact info.

Cheers,
Nick


Thanks,
Marianne

Glad you like it! The stratification
difference is
interesting -- in general, I would hope that
log-likelihoods would improve with more-realistic
constraints, but this doesn't always seem to be
true. I
think it depends on how good the phylogeny
dates are,
how good the geological event dates are, and
whether or
not the constraints really do help explain things
better. And, yes, different models could react
differently to the constraints, which you seem
to have
observed. Makes for an interesting discussion
at least!

Re: d and e (and j etc.) -- currently, these
are global
parameters across all strata, so you would just
have 2
parameters under DEC. Of course, the "meaning"
of d, e,
etc. changes somewhat, in a sense, if they are
operating
under different geographic connectivities in
different
strata. In the extreme case, time-slice 1
might only
allow dispersal between A and B, and time-slice 2
between A, B, C, D, and E. The same "d" will
cause many
more events per unit branch length in
time-slice 2, just
because more events are possible.

One could imagine doing it differently, but
it's hard to
program every special case! It wouldn't be too
hard to
chop up a phylogeny and do different parameters
in each
stratum though...

Cheers!
Nick

No, that should be fine... if I knew
more about
machine precision and how it is set on
various
computers I might have a better answer,
but that
seems to work OK...



My dataset has a very strange and
skewed
geographical
distribution with > 90% of the taxa
in the
Neotropical
region (yellow in attached file)
and the
rest scattered
across the remaining biogeographic
regions.
As you see there
is a lot of uncertainty. I guess
this skewed
dataset might
cause the problems?


Well, actually you've got high
certainty for the
parts of the tree where nothing
changes, which
is most of it, but that's obvious of
course.
The high uncertainty is common for
parts of
the tree where you have widespread
ancestors,
since there are so many different
scenarios
possible at cladogenesis with
widespread ancestors.

It looks like you are running DEC --
often DEC+J
shows a big difference in uncertainty &
likelihood.

Also, it might look somewhat better if
you added
up all of the individual ranges and
just made a
plot of probability of presence in each
area,
adding up the probabilities of each
individual
range. I haven't gotten a chance to do
this and
won't for some time... It would take
some R
skilz and some creative way to display
e.g.
shading for "Prob(occupied)" for each of 6
regions (or whatever) at each node.

Cheers!
Nick
